surveyDefinition.title: Skincare Serums — consumer survey (Global)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 5 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on serum usage patterns, purchase behaviour, ingredient and efficacy priorities, and satisfaction drivers.

segments.name: Clinical Efficacy Buyers
segments.description: High-frequency daily users who prioritise proven, dermatologist-backed results and are willing to pay premium prices for visible anti-aging or skin-improvement outcomes. They research ingredients and clinical evidence before buying.

segments.name: Clean-Conscious Consumers
segments.description: Regular users who prioritise ingredient safety, transparency, and sustainability. They avoid harsh chemicals and prefer fragrance-free, hypoallergenic, and refillable options, even if it means trading some efficacy.

segments.name: Value-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Occasional to regular users who are highly price-sensitive and seek effective serums at accessible price points. They compare options carefully, wait for promotions, and are willing to switch brands for better value.

segments.name: Luxury Experience Buyers
segments.description: High-frequency users who treat serum application as a self-care ritual and are drawn to premium textures, elegant packaging, and brand prestige. They are less price-sensitive and value the sensory experience as much as results.

segments.name: Sensitive-Skin Managers
segments.description: Users who have reactive or sensitive skin and use serums cautiously to address hydration and irritation without triggering breakouts. They prioritise gentle, fragrance-free, hypoallergenic formulations and are wary of new products.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Skincare Serums buyers worldwide. It asks how people use Skincare Serums, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories. This global view is not a separate fieldwork exercise: it selects the strongest questions from the regional surveys and blends their percentages using population-style regional weights.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults worldwide who buy or use Skincare Serums for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased at least one skincare serum in the past 12 months; Individuals who use skincare serums at least once a week; Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own skincare purchases. Excluded: Professional estheticians or dermatologists purchasing for clinical use; Individuals who only use skincare products provided by others (e.g., gifted, part of a subscription box they didn't choose); Individuals under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy skincare serums for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which product to purchase based on their skin concerns and preferences. While some dermatologists may recommend specific serums, the purchase decision and payment are made by the individual consumer, making this a clear B2C market.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly uses skincare products (daily or weekly)
Actively seeks products for specific skin concerns (e.g., anti-aging, hydration, acne)
Informed by social media, beauty influencers, and online reviews
Willing to pay premium prices for perceived efficacy
Tends to repurchase favorite products and experiment with new launches
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Serum Usage & Skin Concerns
sections.covers: Establishes how respondents use serums, their skin concerns, and the role serums play in their routine.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Decision Drivers
sections.covers: Covers what triggers a serum purchase, where they learn about and buy serums, how often they buy, and what decides the choice.

sections.label: Product Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Explores must-have attributes, quality cues, packaging preferences, and the trade-offs they make between efficacy, safety, and price.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Switching Risk
sections.covers: Measures overall satisfaction, what drives it, friction points, switching triggers, and future usage intent.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with serums — whether they use them, for what skin concerns, and how often. It then moves through the purchase journey, from what triggers a buy to where they shop and what ultimately decides the choice. Next, it explores their product requirements, including must-have attributes, quality cues, and the trade-offs they make between efficacy, safety, and price. Finally, it measures satisfaction, friction, switching triggers, and future intent, allowing the data to segment respondents into five behavioural groups based on their usage…

segmentModel.tie_break: Question bb7 (Which of these matters most when you choose a serum?) is the tie-breaker because it directly asks respondents to rank their top priority among the key differentiators (clinical backing, clean ingredients, price, brand, results), making it the most explicit self-report of segment identity.
notes: Frequency questions (cp1, cp6, cp7) help distinguish high-frequency users (clinical, luxury) from occasional users (value) and cautious users (sensitive).
Price questions (bb5, bb6, pe8) are strong discriminators for value-driven and luxury segments.
Ingredient safety and fragrance-free options consistently point to clean-conscious and sensitive-skin segments.
Clinical backing and dermatologist recommendations consistently point to clinical efficacy seekers.
Sensory and brand-related options point to luxury experience seekers.
27 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=250 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
